newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Far East Gold - Physical demand outlook mixed.
newsitem.headline: Far East Gold - Physical demand outlook mixed.

text.p: Some gold traders still clung to hopes of a fourth-quarter seasonal revival, but mounting disappointment with gold's performance and a general slowdown in Asian economic growth has hit demand for physical gold in the region, precious metals traders said on Friday.
Muted physical Asian gold demand despite alluring prices has raised eyebrows in the industry.

"Traditionally, demand at this time should be quite good. The price is so attractive now. India, in particular, has been unusually quiet for the past two to three weeks," a bank trader in Singapore said.
Other traders speculated that physical trade might rise sharply if the price of the yellow metal slid further. They noted demand had not disappeared, it had simply not accelerated.
"The floor right now is somewhere around $378 an ounce, but physical demand in the region is going to kick in if gold falls to around $375 (an ounce)," the trader said.
A European investment house dealer in Singapore said physical demand in the region should begin improving shortly.

"Demand should improve. There's been a bit of professional shortcovering and they've managed to squeeze it up a bit," the dealer said, although he stopped short when asked if a shortcovering rally can be extended into next week.
Others were not so optimistic.
"I don't see an improvement in demand in the short term," said Swiss Bank Corp's chief bullion dealer in Hong Kong, Anderson Cheung.
He noted many Asian countries including China, Taiwan and Japan had bought gold supplies earlier and demand was not as urgent.
"Of course if gold came off $20 (per ounce) we would see very strong demand," Cheung noted.

Bearish sentiment that set in after gold's 5-1/2 year high at $415 per ounce in February this year has been exacerbated recently by lingering International Monetary Fund (IMF) discussions on the possible sale of five million ounces of its gold reserves, other gold dealers said.
Gold premiums in Hong Kong had dropped to 40 U.S. cents on Friday, down from 70 U.S. cents last month when supplies were temporarily tight, sources said.
Hong Kong gold was trading at $380.20/380.70 per ounce at 1430 (0630 GMT).
Dealers said gold's price would be driven mostly by funds in the coming days and not by market fundamentals.
The trader said the large number of short positions in the COMEX gold futures market totalling 5.7 million ounces is especially worrying because of the potential to further weaken the yellow metal.
"If gold breaks $378, it may go all the way down to $371 because there's nothing to support it," he added.
With demand still treading water, Singapore gold premiums over spot London prices slipped slightly to around 30-40 U.S. cents an ounce from 35-45 U.S. cents last week, dealers said.
Within a broader framework, gold demand in Asia has declined as purchasing power in the region was dragged down by slower economic growth in general, traders said.

In January to July 1996, Hong Kong imported 114,376 kgs of gold bullion and coins, compared to 193,307 kgs of bullion and coins imported during the same period last year, according to figures from the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6358
With a contribution from Rene Pastor in Singapore
